video_title: Bitcoin Is Entering Its Most Powerful Wave Ever
gist: Macro investor Jordi Visser tells Anthony Pompliano that rising interest rates won't derail the economy this cycle because AI frontier labs' margins are nearly rate-insensitive and are now the main driver of nominal GDP growth, that money supply will keep outrunning asset values in a slow 'stealth deleveraging' that favors scarce hard assets like Bitcoin, and that AI agents needing crypto-native rails to transact autonomously (not human speculation) is now the primary structural bull case for crypto, while equity market structure itself is already shifting because agent-driven trading no longer rewards blow-out earnings surprises the way human investors used to.

themes.theme: Why Higher Rates Won't Break This Economy

insights.claim: Visser argues a 200 basis point rise in 10-year yields would barely dent profit margins at Anthropic and OpenAI (roughly from 70% to 69% by his estimate), and since these two 'duopoly' frontier AI labs are now the primary driver of nominal GDP growth (over 6%), rate increases of this magnitude are unlikely to meaningfully damage the broader economy the way historical rate-hike cycles did.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If margin sensitivity to rates is genuinely this low for the AI duopoly driving GDP growth, standard 'rates up = risk-asset selloff' playbooks may misfire this cycle — a contrarian reason not to de-risk purely on rate-hike fear.
insights.quote: a 200 basis point rise in 10-year yields doesn't change the margins for Anthropic or Open AI by very much. It's about from let's say 70% to 69%.

insights.claim: Visser distinguishes the level of interest rates from the speed of the move: a slow rise (e.g., over a year) is broadly survivable for the economy, whereas a fast spike (e.g., from 5% to 7% overnight) would immediately force small businesses out and trigger job losses.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Investors should watch the pace of rate changes, not just the terminal level, as the actual risk trigger for economic damage — a specific, testable framework for timing de-risking decisions.
insights.quote: if rates went from 5% to 7% today, because that happened overnight, you'd have a ton of small businesses and things go out of business immediately

insights.claim: Visser believes the U.S. administration (citing Scott Bessent's public commentary, yen-intervention timing, quarterly refunding changes, and expanded buybacks) structurally does not want rates to rise further, regardless of who becomes Fed chair (he floats Kevin Warsh as a possible hawkish pick), because higher rates worsen the government's own interest-expense/debt burden.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If policy is structurally biased toward suppressing real rates regardless of Fed leadership, this favors scarce, non-sovereign assets (Bitcoin, gold) as a hedge against continued financial repression, independent of who chairs the Fed.

insights.claim: Visser cites Stan Druckenmiller's view that rates are being manipulated below their natural level (he argues 10-year yields 'should be' about 8%, roughly 200 basis points above nominal GDP as was historically consistent before 1997) to keep a 'K-shaped' economy from visibly worsening, letting zombie businesses refinance and survive rather than clear out via a recession.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If suppressed real rates are propping up marginal ('zombie') businesses, a later repricing event (when suppression ends) could be sharper than current market pricing implies — a tail risk to monitor even while being bullish on AI-driven growth near-term.
insights.quote: Rates should be more like 8% right now on 10-year yields.

themes.theme: A Contrarian 'Stealth Deleveraging' and Hard-Asset Thesis

insights.claim: Visser presents an original framework in which the classic deleveraging call (asset prices must crash to match a fixed money supply) is wrong; instead he expects the money supply to keep growing while asset values grow more slowly or flatten, gradually normalizing what he estimates is roughly a 7-to-1 ratio between total money (~$100 trillion) and total global asset value (~$700 trillion), driven by AI/humanoid-driven deflation making goods, housing, and labor structurally cheaper over time.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: This reframes the AI-deflation debate away from 'stocks crash' toward 'stocks stagnate in real terms while money printing continues' — implying investors should target scarce, non-inflatable assets rather than broad equity or bond exposure to preserve real purchasing power.
insights.quote: the total sum of all the money, not the value of the assets, but the money, is let's say a hundred trillion dollars. But the value of the assets is seven hundred trillion.

insights.claim: Bitcoin, gold, and land are all up roughly 170% over the trailing five years versus the S&P 500's roughly 70%, which Visser and Pompliano read as evidence that scarce hard assets are capturing the effects of monetary debasement more directly than equities, meaning a large share of 'stock market returns' may just be nominal money-supply growth rather than real gains.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: This comparative return data is a concrete argument for overweighting scarce hard assets (Bitcoin, gold) relative to equities specifically as an inflation/debasement hedge, rather than assuming equities alone provide adequate protection.
insights.quote: Bitcoin, gold, land up about 170% over the last 5 years.

insights.claim: Visser frames the current Bitcoin setup, using Elliott Wave analysis, as the start of a 'third wave' — historically the most powerful phase of a cycle — and argues this requires persistent public disbelief/doubt among prior bulls (citing Mark Cuban publicly souring on crypto) as a necessary psychological precondition, rather than early euphoria, for the move to be genuine.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Persistent skepticism and capitulation among former bulls (rather than broad euphoria) is being used as a specific, checkable sentiment indicator for whether the current Bitcoin rally has more structural room to run.
insights.quote: we're entering a third wave, a big the most powerful wave in crypto.

insights.claim: Visser explicitly rejects the popular 'four-year cycle' narrative that Bitcoin must dip back toward $60,000 before a real bull run, arguing this is a historically-anchored mental bias rather than a fundamental requirement, especially once Bitcoin breaks decisively above the $82,000 level he had previously flagged.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A specific, falsifiable near-term prediction (no return to $60K, sustained break above $82K) that can be tracked against actual Bitcoin price action to evaluate this thesis in real time.

insights.claim: Visser's simplified crypto portfolio framework: Bitcoin as collateral/store of value, Ethereum as the trust layer needed for people to build on-chain, and Solana for speed/transaction throughput — while stating indifference to which other individual tokens outperform.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, three-asset core-holdings framework that simplifies crypto portfolio construction around functional roles (collateral, trust/settlement, speed) rather than trying to pick every outperforming token.
insights.quote: you've got Bitcoin as collateral and store value. You've got Ethereum for kind of the trust that is going to have to happen for people to build on things. And then you're going to have Solana for the speed.

insights.claim: Visser argues holding a 0% weighting in crypto/Bitcoin is logically equivalent to assigning a 0% probability that crypto will ever matter financially, and contends that with AI agents entering the picture and South Korea announcing it will be 'fully tokenized' by February 2027, a 0% allocation is no longer defensible; he advocates a small (implied ~5%) diversified position instead.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A specific allocation argument — reframing 'no crypto position' as an implicit high-conviction bearish bet rather than a neutral default — that financial advisors and RIAs (Visser explicitly targets this audience) could use to justify introducing a small crypto sleeve into traditionally diversified portfolios.
insights.quote: If you have a 0% weighting in crypto in Bitcoin, then you have to assign that you have a 0% probability that crypto is actually going to matter.

themes.theme: AI Agents as the New Structural Bull Case for Crypto

insights.claim: Visser's central reframe is that crypto's bull case is shifting away from human speculation toward AI agents needing to transact instantly, autonomously, and around the clock — something traditional banking rails cannot support — making crypto/stablecoin infrastructure a structural requirement of the agentic economy rather than a speculative bet.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: This reframes crypto's addressable market from retail speculation to agent-to-agent commerce infrastructure, a potentially much larger and more durable demand driver worth tracking via stablecoin transaction volume and agent-payment protocol adoption.
insights.quote: Agents can't do anything on the old rails. It doesn't work.

insights.claim: Visser describes a portfolio-company founder who, about ten weeks before this conversation, switched his B2B SaaS data product from human subscribers to AI-agent subscribers; thousands of agents have since signed up, the average agent now spends over $100/year, and the founder projects $100M+ revenue at 1 million agent customers and $1B+ at 10 million, framing agent acquisition as potentially faster-scaling than human customer acquisition.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, named business-model pivot (sell to agents, not humans) with quantified early revenue-per-agent economics — a specific pattern other B2B SaaS founders and investors should watch for as a new go-to-market category ('agent economy' customers).
insights.quote: The average agent is now spending 100-plus dollars per year with him.

insights.claim: South Korea has announced it will be 'fully tokenized' by February 2027, which Visser cites as evidence that global tokenization is a live policy trend forcing the U.S. (via legislation like the Clarity Act) to keep pace or cede financial infrastructure leadership to other countries.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A specific, dated foreign-policy commitment to full tokenization gives investors a concrete international benchmark and timeline against which to judge whether U.S. tokenization/crypto legislation is falling behind global peers.
insights.quote: South Korea announced that they will be fully tokenized by February of 2027.

insights.claim: Visser argues tokenization will let pension funds and other large allocators finally access small, high-Sharpe-ratio 'AI arbitrage' strategies (currently generating an estimated 18-20%+ annualized with low volatility but too small individually to interest institutional capital) by aggregating thousands of such uncorrelated strategies into a single tokenized basket, similar to a multi-strategy hedge fund platform — though early movers into any individual strategy should expect returns to compress as capital floods in.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Tokenized aggregation of niche AI-driven arbitrage strategies is framed as a concrete, near-term institutional-adoption use case for tokenization beyond simple stock/bond wrapping — a specific product category to watch develop.
insights.quote: if they could find people getting involved in like these little businesses that churn off 20% with low risk, they would love to go through them.

insights.claim: Despite Nvidia guiding next year's revenue growth far above Street consensus (around 70% versus an estimated 44% consensus, which Visser argues implies closer to 100% given the company's size) and Dell issuing a similarly strong pre-announcement, both stocks initially traded down before recovering — which Visser interprets as evidence that the classic 'blow-out guidance = stock pop' playbook is breaking down.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If historically reliable earnings-surprise reactions are no longer working, momentum/reaction-based trading strategies built on that historical pattern need re-calibration — a live market-structure anomaly worth tracking through the next few AI-mega-cap earnings cycles.
insights.quote: your revenue estimates of 44% for next year, they're way too low. We're going to say it's 70.

insights.claim: Visser attributes the changing market reaction pattern partly to AI-agent-driven trading, which he says cares purely about expected value and information edge rather than being 'right' or being rewarded for narrative conviction the way human portfolio managers historically were — a structural shift in who is setting the marginal price.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If agent-driven flow is increasingly setting marginal prices, traditional narrative-driven fundamental investing strategies may need to adapt to a market that prices information faster and less emotionally than before.

insights.claim: Even while expecting continued ~20% annual earnings growth, Visser forecasts persistent equity multiple compression (the index rising only ~7%/year while earnings grow ~20%) alongside more frequent ~20% drawdowns triggered by event risk (e.g., a bank cyberattack), because markets are increasingly questioning terminal value beyond a roughly three-year horizon.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: This is a specific, quantified equity-return forecast (low double-digit price return despite high earnings growth, with fatter tail-risk drawdowns) distinct from simple AI-bull or AI-bear narratives — useful as a testable benchmark for index-level return expectations.
insights.quote: If it goes up at 7% a year while earnings grow at 20%, which is kind of the way I think the multiple compression happens

themes.theme: Managing AI Agents Like Employees, and the 'AGI Is Here' Claim

insights.claim: Visser runs literal daily 'stand-ups' with his AI agents (each reporting what it did yesterday, what it's doing today, and what it's blocked on) and even convened a named 'staff meeting' with his agents when a workflow wasn't producing the output he wanted — explicitly modeling agent management on how he managed human teams at Morgan Stanley and his macro fund.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Treating AI agents with literal human-management processes (stand-ups, staff meetings, named roles) is a specific operational pattern other executives could adopt now to extract more reliable output from multi-agent workflows.
insights.quote: I've had a staff meeting with my agents.

insights.claim: Visser states plainly that 'AGI is here' based on benchmark scores that came close to or hit 100 on a metric defined as the intelligence level needed to replace all human jobs, and separately cites hearing that frontier labs expect the next year of AI model capability improvement to roughly equal the last four years' worth of progress combined.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If capability gains really compress '4 years into 1,' the pace of enterprise/consumer AI-agent adoption and disruption over the next 12 months should be modeled as dramatically faster than trailing-year trends suggest.
insights.quote: AGI is here. That's my takeaway from this week.

insights.claim: Visser argues current compute, memory, and data-center supply constraints are actually beneficial right now because they are slowing the deployment of physical AI/humanoid robotics relative to raw model capability, tempering what he sees as overly aggressive predictions from other commentators (e.g., humanoids driving cars within a year) about the pace of physical-world AI disruption.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A useful counter-narrative to humanoid-robotics hype cycles: physical deployment bottlenecks (compute, memory, data centers) are a real gating factor, suggesting near-term humanoid/autonomous-vehicle timelines from more bullish commentators should be discounted.
